lead: A compression member does not fail by crushing first — it bows sideways, and the load at which it bows is what sizes it. This unit finds that load for real columns, then turns from stability to strength: how a stress state is compared with the yield stress, and how a repeated stress breaks a part that a single load would never break.
about: Unit 3 is about members in compression and about how a stress state becomes a failure. Chapter 3.1 finds the load at which a straight column bows out, and 3.2 gives the Rankine-Gordon fit that joins buckling to crushing for columns of middle length. Chapters 3.3 and 3.4 make the column real: it is never straight, and it yields before it buckles. Chapter 3.5 adds bending to the axial load. Chapters 3.6 and 3.7 change the question from stability to strength and compare a computed stress state with the yield stress using the classical theories. Chapters 3.8 and 3.9 finish with repeated loads: the S-N curve, the endurance limit, and the mean-alternating diagram that turns a fluctuating load into a factor of safety.

chapters.idea: A straight elastic column stays straight until the axial load reaches π²EI/L_e², and above that it bows sideways.
chapters.depth: Derive EI d²v/dx² = −P v for a pinned strut and take the smallest root, P_cr = π²EI/L_e². Define every symbol: E (Young's modulus, Pa), I (second moment of area, m⁴), L_e (effective length, m). List the four end conditions with their effective-length factors K: pinned-pinned 1.0, fixed-fixed 0.5, fixed-pinned 0.7, fixed-free 2.0. Define slenderness λ = L_e/r with radius of gyration r = √(I/A). State the assumptions (straight, homogeneous, elastic, centroidal load, small deflection) and why each one fails on a real aircraft. Note that buckling happens about the weaker axis. Some syllabi call this Euler's theory or the critical load of a strut. Use: engine-mount tubes, truss-rib struts.

root.label: Column ends
root.note: K and P for the 2 m strut

figure.aria: A tree of four column end conditions, each box giving the effective-length factor and the buckling load of the 2 m aluminium strut in the worked example.

chapters.example: An aluminium strut has E = 70 GPa, length L = 2.0 m, I = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m⁴ and A = 500 mm², pinned at both ends. Find the buckling load and the slenderness ratio, then repeat for the other three end conditions. Answer: P_cr = π²EI/L² = 9.8696 × 70×10⁹ × 2.0×10⁻⁷ / 2.0² = 34 543 N ≈ 34.5 kN. r = √(I/A) = √(2.0×10⁻⁷ / 5.0×10⁻⁴) = 0.020 m = 20 mm, so λ = L_e/r = 2000/20 = 100. The mean stress 34.5 kN / 500 mm² = 69 MPa is far below the yield of aluminium alloy, so the elastic formula is valid. Fixed-fixed: K = 0.5, P_cr = 34.5/0.5² = 138 kN. Fixed-pinned: K = 0.7, P_cr = 34.5/0.7² = 70.4 kN. Fixed-free: K = 2.0, P_cr = 34.5/4 = 8.6 kN.
chapters.trap: Putting the full length L into π²EI/L² when the ends are not pinned, and taking I about the stronger axis so that the column buckles about the other one first.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for beam deflection and Unit 1 for where struts sit in a truss rib.
chapters.leave: Inelastic buckling to 3.4, imperfect columns to 3.3, and plate or local buckling to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Rankine-Gordon joins the crushing load and the Euler load in one formula, so a column of middle length is credited with neither the full squash load nor the full Euler load.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in the structures paper, so keep it short. Build 1/P_R = 1/P_c + 1/P_E, where P_c = σ_c A is the crushing (squash) load and P_E is the Euler load, and rearrange to P_R = σ_c A/(1 + a λ²) with a = σ_c/(π²E). Show that the formula tends to P_c for short columns and to P_E for long ones, and never exceeds either. Give the stress form σ_R = σ_c/(1 + aλ²). Some syllabi call it the Rankine formula or the Gordon-Rankine formula. Say that a is usually taken from tests or a handbook, and that λ must use L_e.

figure.aria: Two curves against slenderness: the Euler load falling steeply from very high values, and the Rankine-Gordon load flattening out at the crushing load of 128 kN.

chapters.example: A pinned steel strut is 600 mm long with A = 400 mm², I = 1.0×10⁴ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa and a crushing stress σ_c = 320 MPa. Find r, λ, the Euler load and the Rankine-Gordon load. Answer: r = √(I/A) = √(10⁴/400) = 5 mm, L_e = 600 mm, λ = 120. P_c = σ_c A = 320 × 400 = 128 kN. P_E = π²EI/L_e² = 9.8696 × 200×10⁹ × 1.0×10⁻⁸ / 0.36 = 54.8 kN. a = σ_c/(π²E) = 320/(9.8696 × 200 000) = 1.62×10⁻⁴. P_R = 128/(1 + 1.62×10⁻⁴ × 120²) = 128/3.33 = 38.4 kN.
chapters.trap: Mixing units inside the constant a (σ_c and E must be in the same unit) and using the true length instead of L_e inside λ.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the Euler load and the slenderness ratio.
chapters.leave: The derivation of Euler to 3.1 and true inelastic behaviour to 3.4.

chapters.idea: A real strut is slightly bowed or slightly off-centre, and the bending that offset causes is multiplied by sec((π/2)√(P/P_E)), which grows without limit at the Euler load.
chapters.depth: Treat initial curvature and load eccentricity e as the same problem: an initial bow of amplitude a behaves like an eccentricity. Set up EI d²v/dx² + Pv = −P e and solve to get the secant formula σ_max = (P/A)[1 + (ec/r²) sec((L_e/2)√(P/EI))]. Rewrite the argument as (π/2)√(P/P_E) so the blow-up at P_E is visible. Define the amplification factor and show it is 1 when P is small. Explain the engineering response: allow a measured bow, and design to σ_max not σ_avg. Name Perry-Robertson as the same idea written as an empirical column curve. Use: stringer straightness limits, jacking a fuselage frame.

figure.title: How an eccentricity feeds itself
figure.aria: A flow that starts with an off-centre load, produces a primary moment, causes a deflection, and feeds a second moment back into that deflection until the secant formula gives the peak stress.

chapters.example: A pinned aluminium strut is 1.0 m long with E = 70 GPa, A = 200 mm², I = 2.0×10⁴ mm⁴ and c = 10 mm. The load P = 8 kN acts 2 mm off the centroidal axis. Find the maximum compressive stress and the amplification over P/A. Answer: r = √(I/A) = √(2.0×10⁴/200) = 10 mm. P_E = π²EI/L² = 9.8696 × 70×10⁹ × 2.0×10⁻⁸ / 1.0² = 13 817 N = 13.8 kN. P/A = 8000/200×10⁻⁶ = 40 MPa. ec/r² = (2 × 10)/100 = 0.20. (L/2)√(P/EI) = 0.5 × √(8000/1400) = 1.195 rad. sec(1.195) = 1/cos(1.195) = 2.73. σ_max = 40 × (1 + 0.20 × 2.73) = 40 × 1.546 = 61.8 MPa, an amplification of 1.55 on the mean stress.
chapters.trap: Computing the secant in degrees instead of radians, and forgetting the leading P/A term so that the answer comes out as bending stress only.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for P_E and chapter 3.3 needs nothing from Unit 2 beyond simple beam bending.
chapters.leave: Inelastic magnification to 3.4 and the axial-plus-bending interaction to 3.5.

chapters.idea: Once the stress in a column passes the proportional limit, the material's tangent stiffness E_t is less than E, so the column buckles below the Euler load.
chapters.depth: Show that buckling uses the slope of the stress-strain curve at the working stress, not the initial E. Give Engesser's tangent-modulus load P_cr = π²E_t I/L_e² and Kármán's reduced-modulus (double-modulus) value E_r, then state Shanley's result that the true bifurcation happens at E_t on a rising load path. Define the proportional limit and the transition slenderness λ_t = √(π²E/σ_prop) above which Euler is valid. Give Johnson's parabolic formula σ_cr = σ_y − (σ_y²/(4π²E))λ², valid up to λ_t = √(2π²E/σ_y), and show it touches the Euler curve there. Mention that very short, thin-walled members fail by local buckling or crippling instead — that is Unit 6.

figure.aria: A parabola falling from 320 MPa at zero slenderness and an Euler hyperbola falling from high values, the two touching at a slenderness of about 66 and a stress of 160 MPa, with the worked example marked at slenderness 40.

chapters.example: An aluminium alloy strut has E = 70 GPa, σ_y = 320 MPa, A = 300 mm² and r = 5 mm. It is pinned at both ends with L = 0.20 m. Find the buckling stress and load, and compare with Euler. Answer: λ = L_e/r = 200/5 = 40. Transition slenderness λ_t = √(2π²E/σ_y) = √(2 × 690 870/320) = √4318 = 65.7, so λ < λ_t and the column is inelastic. Johnson constant = σ_y²/(4π²E) = 320²/(4 × 9.8696 × 70 000) = 0.03706. σ_cr = 320 − 0.03706 × 40² = 320 − 59.3 = 260.7 MPa. Load = 260.7 × 300 = 78.2 kN. Euler would give 690 870/1600 = 431.8 MPa, which is above yield and therefore invalid.
chapters.trap: Using Euler above the proportional limit, and quoting E_r as the buckling modulus when Shanley's argument says the tangent modulus E_t is the one that starts the buckle.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2 for the elastic load and the slenderness ratio.
chapters.leave: Crippling of short flanges and local buckling to Unit 6; plasticity in bending is not covered here.

chapters.idea: An axial compression on a beam multiplies its bending moments, so a beam-column is designed with amplified moments, not the first-order ones.
chapters.depth: Set up EI d²v/dx² + Pv = −M(x) for a member with axial load P and transverse load or end moments. Solve for the simply supported case with a central load to get M_max = M_0/(1 − P/P_E), where M_0 is the first-order moment and P_E the Euler load of the same member. Give the secant form for end moments. State the limits: the amplification factor is for a sine-shaped deflection, so it is close for a central load and approximate otherwise. Present the interaction check P/P_cr + M/M_u ≤ 1 and explain that the amplified moment is used inside it. Use: a fuselage stringer taking pressurisation bending plus axial load, a lower wing spar panel.

figure.aria: The moment amplification rising steeply towards the Euler load while the first-order moment stays flat, with the worked example marked at a load ratio of 0.51 and an amplification of 2.03.

chapters.example: A simply supported stringer of length 1.0 m carries 15 kN of axial compression and a transverse load that alone gives M_0 = 0.05 kN m at mid-span. Take EI = 3000 N m², A = 250 mm², I = 3.6×10⁴ mm⁴ and c = 12 mm. Find the peak stress. Answer: P_E = π²EI/L² = 9.8696 × 3000/1.0² = 29 609 N = 29.6 kN. P/P_E = 15/29.6 = 0.507. Amplification = 1/(1 − 0.507) = 2.03. M_max = 2.03 × 0.05 = 0.101 kN m. Axial stress = 15 000/250×10⁻⁶ = 60 MPa. Bending stress = M c/I = 101 × 0.012/3.6×10⁻⁸ = 33.8 MPa. Peak stress = 93.8 MPa.
chapters.trap: Adding the axial stress and the first-order bending stress and stopping there; the axial load also increases the moment, which is where most of the danger lies.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for beam deflection, chapter 3.1 for the Euler load and chapter 3.3 for the idea of amplification.
chapters.leave: Flexural-torsional buckling of thin-walled columns to Unit 6, and shear flow in the same section to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A stress state is called safe when its largest principal stress, or its largest principal strain, stays below the value that causes yield in a simple tension test.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in the structures paper, so keep it compact. Define the three principal stresses and the three principal strains with Hooke's law in 3D: ε1 = (σ1 − νσ2 − νσ3)/E. Maximum principal stress theory (Rankine): failure when σ1 reaches σ_yt in tension or σ3 reaches −σ_yc in compression. Maximum principal strain theory (St Venant): failure when the largest of |ε1|, |ε2|, |ε3| reaches σ_y/E. Give the 2D form ε1 = (σ1 − νσ2)/E and the safe-region shapes. Say that both are poor for ductile metals and better for brittle ones, and that the strain theory is still used for some composite and cast parts.

figure.title: Two theories from one stress state
figure.aria: A flow from a plane stress state to the principal stresses, then down two branches, one comparing principal stress with yield and one comparing principal strain, both ending in a factor of safety.

chapters.example: At a point in an aluminium alloy panel σx = 100 MPa, σy = −40 MPa, τxy = 30 MPa. Take σ_y = 250 MPa, ν = 0.3. Find the factor of safety by the maximum principal stress and maximum principal strain theories. Answer: σ_avg = (100 − 40)/2 = 30 MPa, R = √(70² + 30²) = √5800 = 76.2 MPa, so σ1 = 106.2 MPa and σ2 = −46.2 MPa. Principal stress theory: 106.2 < 250, factor = 250/106.2 = 2.36. Principal strain theory: ε1E = σ1 − νσ2 = 106.2 + 13.8 = 120.0 MPa; ε2E = σ2 − νσ1 = −46.2 − 31.9 = −78.1 MPa; ε3E = −ν(σ1 + σ2) = −18.0 MPa. Largest magnitude is 120.0 MPa, factor = 250/120.0 = 2.08.
chapters.trap: Using the 2D strain formula when a third principal stress exists, and comparing the signed principal stress with yield instead of its magnitude.
chapters.prereq: Mohr's circle and principal stresses from the stress analysis covered in Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Shear and distortion-energy theories to 3.7, and repeated loading to 3.9.

chapters.idea: A ductile metal yields when the shear stress, or the distortion energy, reaches the value measured in a tension test, and Tresca and von Mises bracket the answer.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this here, so keep it tight. Maximum shear stress theory (Tresca): failure when the largest of |σ1 − σ2|, |σ2 − σ3|, |σ3 − σ1| reaches σ_y. Distortion energy theory (von Mises): σ_eq = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) for plane stress and the full three-term form in 3D; in stress components σ_eq = √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²). Octahedral shear theory: τ_oct = (1/3)√((σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)²), with σ_eq = (3/√2)τ_oct, which shows von Mises is the octahedral shear criterion. Compare the three on one stress state and note that Tresca is conservative.

figure.aria: Three equivalent-stress curves rising with shear stress for a fixed stress state, Tresca highest, von Mises in the middle and maximum principal stress lowest, all three passing their values at 30 MPa shear.

chapters.example: At a point in a ductile panel σx = 100 MPa, σy = −40 MPa, τxy = 30 MPa and σ_y = 250 MPa. Compare the three theories and give each factor of safety. Answer: σ_avg = 30 MPa, R = √(70² + 30²) = 76.2 MPa, so σ1 = 106.2 MPa, σ2 = −46.2 MPa, σ3 = 0. Tresca: σ_eq = σ1 − σ2 = 152.3 MPa, factor = 250/152.3 = 1.64. von Mises: σ_eq = √(100² − 100×(−40) + 40² + 3×30²) = √18 300 = 135.3 MPa, factor = 250/135.3 = 1.85. Octahedral shear: τ_oct = (1/3)√(152.3² + 46.2² + 106.2²) = 63.8 MPa, and (3/√2) × 63.8 = 135.3 MPa, the same von Mises value. Maximum principal stress would give 250/106.2 = 2.36, which is not safe to use for a ductile metal.
chapters.trap: Taking only σ1 − σ2 for Tresca when σ3 = 0 and σ2 is negative, so the largest difference is a different pair.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.6 for principal stresses and strains.
chapters.leave: Fatigue and mean stress to 3.9; yield criteria for orthotropic composite plies to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A stress well below yield will still break a part if it repeats often enough, and the number of cycles to failure is read from the S-N curve.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in the structures paper. Define fatigue as crack initiation and growth under repeated stress, and distinguish high-cycle from low-cycle behaviour without going into strain-life detail. Define the S-N curve (Wöhler curve): stress amplitude S against cycles to failure N, plotted on a log scale for N. Define the endurance limit (fatigue limit) as the stress below which the material survives indefinitely, reached near 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles for steels; state that aluminium and most non-ferrous alloys show no true limit and are quoted at a fixed life instead. Give Basquin's power law S = A N^b and show how b is found from two points. List the factors that lower the limit: surface finish, size, notches, corrosion, mean stress (pointer to 3.9).

figure.aria: The S-N line falling from 600 MPa at a thousand cycles to 400 MPa at a million cycles, where it meets the flat endurance-limit line.

chapters.example: A steel has an ultimate strength of 800 MPa. Rotating-bending tests give a fatigue strength of 600 MPa at 10³ cycles and 400 MPa at 10⁶ cycles, and the strength stays at 400 MPa beyond that. Fit Basquin's law and find the life at 500 MPa. Answer: S = A N^b, so log 600 = log A + 3b and log 400 = log A + 6b. Subtract: b = (2.602 − 2.778)/3 = −0.0587. Then log A = 2.778 + 3(0.0587) = 2.954, so A = 900 MPa. S = 900 N^(−0.0587). At S = 500 MPa: log(500/900) = −0.0587 log N, so log N = 0.2553/0.0587 = 4.35 and N = 2.2×10⁴ cycles. The endurance limit is 400 MPa, half the ultimate strength.
chapters.trap: Reading cycles on a linear axis, and assuming an endurance limit exists for an aluminium alloy when it does not.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.7 for what counts as a safe stress when the load is steady.
chapters.leave: Mean-stress correction to 3.9; cumulative damage and crack-growth laws to a later fatigue course.

chapters.idea: A fluctuating stress splits into a steady mean part and an alternating part, and a constant-life diagram combines both into one factor of safety.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this here. Define σ_max, σ_min, σ_m = (σ_max + σ_min)/2 and σ_a = (σ_max − σ_min)/2, the stress ratio R = σ_min/σ_max and the amplitude ratio A = σ_a/σ_m. Show the special cases: R = −1 is fully reversed, R = 0 is zero to maximum, R = 1 is steady. Build the constant-life (Haigh) diagram with σ_m on one axis and σ_a on the other. Give the three lines: Goodman σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_u = 1, Gerber σ_a/S_e + (σ_m/S_u)² = 1, Soderberg σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_y = 1, and the Langer yield line σ_a + σ_m = S_y. Explain that Goodman is the usual conservative choice, Gerber fits ductile data better, and Soderberg is the most conservative. Show the factor of safety n as the factor by which both stresses are scaled.

figure.aria: Three constant-life lines falling from an alternating stress of 400 MPa to zero, Soderberg the steepest, Gerber the outermost, with the worked load point at a mean of 100 MPa and an alternating stress of 200 MPa.

chapters.example: A steel part sees σ_max = 300 MPa and σ_min = −100 MPa. Take S_e = 400 MPa, S_u = 800 MPa and S_y = 600 MPa. Find σ_m, σ_a, R and the factor of safety by Goodman, Soderberg and Gerber. Answer: σ_m = (300 − 100)/2 = 100 MPa, σ_a = (300 + 100)/2 = 200 MPa, R = −100/300 = −0.33, A = 200/100 = 2.0. Goodman: 1/n = 200/400 + 100/800 = 0.625, n = 1.60. Soderberg: 1/n = 200/400 + 100/600 = 0.667, n = 1.50. Gerber: 0.5n + (0.125n)² = 1, so 0.0156n² + 0.5n − 1 = 0 and n = 1.89. First-cycle yielding is checked by σ_a + σ_m = 300 MPa < S_y = 600 MPa, so yield does not govern.
chapters.trap: Dividing S_e by σ_a alone when there is a tensile mean stress, and getting the sign of R wrong by using σ_max/σ_min.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.8 for the endurance limit, and chapter 3.6 for combining stresses at a point.
chapters.leave: Notch and surface corrections to 3.8; cumulative damage to a later fatigue course.
